chapters.core_summary: Introduces the fundamental concept of congruence of plane figures, specifically focusing on geometric symbols and triangles. It explores superimposition, rotation, and reflection, and defines corresponding vertices, sides, and angles. It examines the minimum criteria needed to establish triangle congruence (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) and establishes the strict convention for vertex order in congruence notation.
key_concepts: Congruence of Plane Figures (identical shape and size)
Superimposition, Rotation, and Reflection testing
Corresponding Vertices, Corresponding Sides, and Corresponding Angles
Strict Vertex Correspondence in Congruence Notation (e.g., ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ)
Minimal Conditions for Triangle Congruence (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS)
Application of Congruence in Real-World Designs and Cardboard Cutouts

key_terms.definition: Geometric figures that have the exact same shape and size, matching perfectly when superimposed over each other.
Placing one geometric figure directly over another to check if they coincide completely.
Pairs of vertices from two congruent figures that align with each other upon superimposition.
Pairs of sides from two congruent figures that match in position and have equal lengths.
Pairs of angles from two congruent figures that match in position and have equal measures.
Side-Angle-Side congruence rule stating two triangles are congruent if two sides and the included angle of one equal those of the other.
Side-Side-Side congruence rule stating two triangles are congruent if all three sides of one equal the corresponding three sides of the other.
Angle-Side-Angle congruence rule stating two triangles are congruent if two angles and the included side of one equal those of the other.
Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side congruence rule for right-angled triangles.

key_takeaways: Two figures are congruent if they share identical shape and size, regardless of orientation (rotation or flip).
Congruence notation strictly preserves vertex mapping (e.g., ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ implies A corresponds to X, B to Y, C to Z).
Establishing triangle congruence requires testing minimal sets of measurements (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) rather than all six components.
Once congruence is proven, all corresponding sides and corresponding angles are guaranteed to be equal.

chapters.core_summary: Explores the multiplication and division of positive and negative integers using physical models such as token bags (red/green tokens) and number-line movement models. It derives the rules of signs for multiplication, analyzes patterns in integer sequences, establishes algebraic properties (commutative, associative, distributive), and addresses integer division rules and numerical expressions.
key_concepts: Modeling Integers using Movement and Magnitude (distance and direction from zero)
Token Bag Model for Multiplication (adding vs. removing positive/negative tokens)
Rules of Signs in Integer Multiplication (same signs yield positive; opposite signs yield negative)
Patterns in Integer Sequences and Multiplicative Decrements
Distributive Property of Multiplication over Addition: a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c)
Integer Division and Quotients with Positive and Negative Numbers
Additive Inverse and Multiplicative Relationships in Expressions

key_terms.definition: The distance or absolute numerical value of a number from zero, independent of its positive or negative sign.
The quantity or number that is subject to multiplication.
The quantity that indicates how many times the multiplicand is added to or removed from a set.
The property stating that multiplying a sum by a number gives the same result as multiplying each addend separately and adding the products.
The number that, when added to a given integer, yields a sum of zero (e.g., -4 for 4).
The total number or quantity that is divided by the divisor.
The result obtained by dividing one number by another.

key_takeaways: A positive multiplier corresponds to adding token sets, while a negative multiplier corresponds to removing token sets.
Multiplying integers with identical signs yields a positive product; multiplying integers with opposite signs yields a negative product.
The distributive property holds across all integers including negative values and zero.
Division by negative integers follows sign rules analogous to multiplication.

chapters.core_summary: Deals with factors, multiples, Highest Common Factor (HCF / GCD), and Least Common Multiple (LCM). It connects arithmetic operations to practical spatial problems (tiling room floors with square tiles, packaging commodities), introduces prime factorisation, demonstrates simultaneous procedures for calculating HCF and LCM, and introduces formal mathematical terms like generalisation and conjecture.
key_concepts: Factors, Common Factors, and Highest Common Factor (HCF / GCD)
Multiples, Common Multiples, and Least Common Multiple (LCM)
Simultaneous HCF and LCM Calculation using Prime Factorisation
Generalisations and Algebraic Representations of Number Patterns
Properties of HCF and LCM for Consecutive, Even, and Co-prime Numbers
Scaling Behavior of HCF and LCM (e.g., doubling numbers doubles their HCF)

key_terms.definition: The largest factor shared in common by two or more integers; also called Greatest Common Divisor (GCD).
The smallest positive integer that is divisible by two or more given integers.
A general statement that describes a mathematical pattern or property holding true across all valid cases.
A mathematical statement or hypothesis proposed as true based on observed patterns but awaiting formal proof.
Pairs of numbers that share no common factor other than 1 (HCF = 1).
Writing a composite number as a product of its prime factors.

key_takeaways: HCF provides the maximum dimension in spatial partitioning problems (such as largest square tiles covering a rectangle).
If one number divides another, their HCF is the smaller number and their LCM is the larger number.
For co-prime numbers, the HCF is 1 and the LCM is equal to their direct product.
Simultaneous division procedures streamline finding HCF and LCM together.

chapters.core_summary: Extends place-value knowledge to advanced decimal operations, focusing on decimal multiplication and division. It examines place-value fraction representations (tenths, hundredths, thousandths), establishes place-value division algorithms, explores relationships between dividends, divisors, and quotients (including division by numbers less than 1), and applies decimals to calendar years (Earth's orbit of 365.2422 days) and commercial word problems.
key_concepts: Decimal Place Value System (Tenths 0.1, Hundredths 0.01, Thousandths 0.001)
Multiplication of Decimals using Whole-Number Products and Decimal Place Tracking
Product Behavior when Factors are Between 0 and 1
Division of Decimals via Equivalent Power-of-10 Fractions
Division using Place Value Decomposition (Thousands, Hundreds, Tens, Ones, Tenths)
Dividend, Divisor, and Quotient Dynamics (Quotients exceeding Dividends when Divisor < 1)
Real-World Scientific and Financial Calculations (e.g., Earth revolution 365.2422 days)

key_terms.definition: One part in ten equal parts of a whole (0.1 or 1/10).
One part in one hundred equal parts of a whole (0.01 or 1/100).
Fractions that express the same numerical value or proportion despite different numerators and denominators.
A quotient that includes decimal places resulting from division beyond whole numbers.
The number by which another number (dividend) is divided.
The number or quantity that is divided.

key_takeaways: Multiplying decimals is executed as whole-number multiplication, placing the decimal point according to the sum of factor decimal places.
Dividing a number by a positive decimal less than 1 yields a quotient greater than the original dividend.
Converting decimals into equivalent power-of-10 fractions standardizes complex division into simple whole-number operations.
Precise decimal operations enable modeling astronomical and financial realities accurately.

chapters.core_summary: Introduces statistical thinking, data collection, and central tendency measures. It covers statistical vs. non-statistical questions, calculation and comparison of Arithmetic Mean and Median, graphical representation via dot plots and clustered bar graphs, analysis of outliers and their effect on mean versus median, and systematic two-step graph interpretation applied to real-world datasets.
key_concepts: Statistical Questions vs. Non-Statistical Questions
Measures of Central Tendency: Arithmetic Mean and Median
Data Variability and Graphical Distribution using Dot Plots
Outliers: Definition and Impact on Mean vs. Median (Resistance of Median)
Clustered and Double-Bar Graphs for Multi-Category and Time-Series Data
Two-Step Graph Interpretation Method (Identify Given -> Infer and Synthesize)
Historical Context of Averages (e.g., European 16-foot land measurement rod)

key_terms.definition: The branch of mathematics dealing with collecting, organizing, analyzing, interpreting, and presenting data.
A question that anticipates and accounts for variability in the data gathered to answer it.
The sum of all values in a dataset divided by the total count of values.
The middle value in an ordered dataset; if the count is even, the average of the two central numbers.
An extreme observation in a dataset that lies unusually far from other values.
A simple chart that displays individual data points as dots above a number line to show shape and spread.
A graph that groups multiple related bars side by side to compare different categories across variables or time.

key_takeaways: Statistical questions require collecting data exhibiting variability rather than single deterministic answers.
Mean is sensitive to extreme values (outliers), whereas median is robust and better represents skewed data distributions.
Graph interpretation requires observing scale, grouping, and ordering before making logical inferences.
Clustered bar graphs facilitate multi-dimensional comparative analysis.

chapters.core_summary: Covers practical geometry using an unmarked ruler and compass. It guides students through constructing perpendicular bisectors, right angles (90°), angle bisectors, copying angles, parallel lines, regular polygons (equilateral triangles, squares, regular hexagons), pointed arches, curved symmetric designs ('Eyes'), and introduces grid tiling (tessellations) without gaps or overlaps.
key_concepts: Construction using Unmarked Ruler and Compass
Construction of Perpendicular Bisectors and Segment Midpoints
Right Angle Construction (90°) and Angle Bisection
Copying Angles and Constructing Parallel Lines
Special Angles (60°, 120°) and Regular Hexagon Constructions
Curved Symmetric Designs and Pointed Arches via Supporting Lines
Tiling (Tessellation) of Grids using Repeating Shapes without gaps or overlaps

key_terms.definition: Drawing precise lines, angles, and shapes using only an unmarked straightedge ruler and a compass.
A line that divides a line segment into two equal segments at a 90° right angle.
Dividing a geometric entity (line segment or angle) into two equal parts.
A closed 2D polygon with all sides equal in length and all interior angles equal in measure.
Covering a two-dimensional region completely using repeating geometric shapes with no gaps and no overlaps.
A dissection puzzle consisting of seven flat polygon pieces arranged to form shapes.

key_takeaways: Geometrical constructions rely on fundamental properties of circles, equal radii, and triangle congruence conditions.
Every point on a perpendicular bisector is equidistant from the endpoints of the line segment.
Artistic and architectural figures (arches, rosettes) are systematically built using underlying supporting lines and arcs.
Shapes whose interior angles fit evenly around 360° can tile a plane seamlessly without gaps or overlaps.

chapters.core_summary: Introduces elementary algebra and simple equations. It uses visual balance scales (weighing balances, mobile hanging scales) and operation/function machines to conceptualize algebraic unknowns, variables (using letters like x, y), algebraic expressions, and linear equations. It details methods for solving equations by maintaining equality symmetrically on both sides of the equal sign.
key_concepts: Concept of Unknowns and Variables (represented by symbols, letters)
Visual Balance Models (Weighing scales, hanging mobiles as balanced equations)
Function/Operation Machines (Input-Output operations and reverse chains)
Algebraic Expressions versus Algebraic Equations
Maintenance of Equality (performing identical operations on LHS and RHS)
Solving Linear Equations using Inverse Operations and Transposition
Translating Practical Word Problems into Equations (e.g., taxi rates, blob puzzles)

key_terms.definition: A letter or symbol used to represent an unknown numerical value in algebraic expressions and equations.
A mathematical phrase that combines numbers, variables, and operational signs (e.g., 2x + 10).
A mathematical statement declaring that two algebraic expressions are equal (LHS = RHS).
The specific numerical value of a variable that makes the equation true (LHS equals RHS).
Left Hand Side and Right Hand Side of an algebraic equation.
An operation that reverses the effect of another operation (e.g., subtraction reverses addition; division reverses multiplication).

key_takeaways: An equation functions like a balanced scale; preserving equality requires performing the exact same operation on both sides.
Solving for an unknown requires isolating the variable by systematically applying inverse operations.
Operation machines illustrate how forward operational steps can be reversed to determine initial inputs.
Real-world word problems can be modeled algebraically to solve for unknown quantities.
